# taxodist

Taxonomic hierarchy distances and lineage analysis in R, Python, and Julia
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-3 .text-center}
![](images/taxodist_sepia.png){.homepage-logo width="160" fig-alt="taxodist logo"}
:::
:::

[![CRAN status](https://img.shields.io/cran/v/taxodist?color=green)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=taxodist) &nbsp; [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/taxodist?color=green)](https://pypi.org/project/taxodist) &nbsp; [![JuliaHub version](https://juliahub.com/docs/Taxodist/version.svg)](https://platform.juliahub.com/ui/Packages/General/Taxodist/)

`taxodist` retrieves ordered taxonomic lineages from [The Taxonomicon](http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl) and compares hierarchy nodes through the depth of their most recent common ancestor (MRCA). The R, Python, and Julia packages implement the same distance definition and lineage semantics.

[Usage guide](getting-started.qmd) · [Web application](https://3w6g1b-rodrigo-villa.shinyapps.io/taxodist_app/) · [Function reference](reference.qmd)

## What does taxodist measure?

For two ordered lineages, `taxodist` finds their continuous common prefix. The final node in that prefix is their MRCA. Distance is then defined as

$$
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & \text{if the complete lineages of } A \text{ and } B \text{ are identical}, \\
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA}(A,B))}, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

A deeper shared ancestor produces a smaller distance. Zero is reserved for identical hierarchy nodes; distinct nodes always have a positive distance, including when one taxon is an ancestor of the other.

::: {.callout-important title="Classification distance, not evolutionary distance"}
The values describe separation in a taxonomic classification. They are **not** evolutionary time, genetic distance, morphological divergence, or phylogenetic branch length. Dendrograms produced from the matrix summarize these classification distances and must not be interpreted as inferred phylogenetic trees.
:::

Within the Taxonomicon hierarchy, depth begins at 1 for `Biota`, so distinct valid nodes have distances in $(0,1]$. The definition is an ultrametric. Taxa whose lineages cannot be retrieved produce missing values in multi-taxon results; infinite distance is retained only as a defensive result for disconnected input lineages.

[Methodology](methodology.qmd)

::: {.callout-note title="Release 0.7.0"}
Version 0.7.0 optimizes cached matrix construction while preserving the public API and distance semantics. All implementations use streamlined numeric pairwise paths and reuse resolved lineages more efficiently; R now fills compact `dist` storage directly, Python reuses HTTP connections, and Julia more completely parses intermediate hierarchy nodes. Cross-language validation confirmed matching resolved identifiers, lineage audits, and matrix values.
:::

## Software interfaces

| Interface | Distribution | Principal output |
|---|---|---|
| R | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=taxodist) and [source code](https://github.com/rodrigosqrt3/taxodist) | Base R `dist` objects and S3 analysis methods |
| Python | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/taxodist) and [source code](https://github.com/rodrigosqrt3/taxodist-py) | Labeled `pandas` objects and analysis dictionaries |
| Julia | [JuliaHub](https://platform.juliahub.com/ui/Packages/General/Taxodist/) and [source code](https://github.com/rodrigosqrt3/taxodist-jl) | Labeled `TaxonomicDistanceMatrix` objects and native named tuples |
| Web application | [Interactive interface](https://3w6g1b-rodrigo-villa.shinyapps.io/taxodist_app/) | Browser-based lineage and distance exploration |

## Basic workflow

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
library(taxodist)

taxa <- c(
  "Tyrannosaurus",
  "Velociraptor",
  "Triceratops",
  "Homo sapiens"
)

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage <- get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result <- taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result$mrca
result$distance

# Build and analyze a community matrix
mat <- distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster <- taxo_cluster(mat)
ordination <- taxo_ordinate(mat)

plot(cluster)
plot(ordination)
```

### Python

```python
import taxodist as td

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage = td.get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result = td.taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result["mrca"]
result["distance"]

# Build and analyze a community matrix
matrix = td.distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster = td.taxo_cluster(matrix)
ordination = td.taxo_ordinate(matrix)
```

### Julia

```julia
using Taxodist

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage = get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result = taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result.mrca
result.distance

# Build and analyze a community matrix
matrix = distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster = taxo_cluster(matrix)
ordination = taxo_ordinate(matrix)
```

:::

## Core API

| Task | Functions |
|---|---|
| Retrieve and resolve taxa | `get_lineage()`, `get_lineage_by_id()`, `get_taxonomicon_id()`, `taxo_search()` |
| Compare two lineages | `taxo_distance()`, `mrca()`, `shared_clades()`, `compare_lineages()`, `taxo_path()` |
| Work with communities | `distance_matrix()`, `focal_distances()`, `closest_relative()`, `check_coverage()` |
| Test clade membership | `is_member()`, `filter_clade()` |
| Analyze and visualize | `taxo_cluster()`, `taxo_ordinate()`, `taxo_heatmap()` |
| Manage retrieval caches | `cache_info()`, `save_cache()`, `load_cache()`, `clear_cache()` |
| Load the offline reference object | `load_taxobase()` |

## Reproducible reference data

R provides the `taxobase` data object, while Python and Julia provide `load_taxobase()`. Release 0.7.0 preserves the same component structure, taxon order, matrices, examples, and provenance metadata across the three implementations, using native containers in each language.

This object is useful for demonstrations, tests, and reproducible examples that should not depend on live network access. Live Taxonomicon queries may change as the underlying classification is updated.

## Data source and citation

All retrieved lineage data originate from **The Taxonomicon**, based on *Systema Naturae 2000*. Published analyses should cite both the `taxodist` software and the underlying classification source:

> Brands, S.J. (1989 onwards). *Systema Naturae 2000*. Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Retrieved from The Taxonomicon, <http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl>.
